summary:
Kai Hendry and Vincent De Smet explore how coding agents change the economics of building software, the work of infrastructure engineers and the processes that surround a release. Anthropic’s Scion source-control system provides a concrete example, but the hosts disagree about how quickly other enterprises can adopt similar ways of working.

[slide:1]

### [00:03:04] Source control designed for agents

Vincent walks through Anthropic’s engineering article on Scion. The discussion focuses on always-online clients, the separation between client and server capabilities, and fetching only the repository data an agent needs. Kai asks how this fits with background agents moving away from developers’ laptops and into shared cloud environments.

From [00:07:29], they discuss the Agent Client Protocol, Kiro and the distinction between an agent harness and its user interface. The conversation then turns to Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode: how much of the experience comes from the model, and how much comes from the tools and interface around it?

[slide:2]

### [00:14:06] When an engineer needs to say no

Anthropic’s account of engineers steering agents prompts a discussion about rules and adversarial reviews. Strict instructions can push an agent towards workarounds, excessive validation and unnecessary complexity. Kai describes a sandbox restriction that leaked into application code; Vincent argues that engineers need to recognise when a rule has stopped helping.

The hosts also discuss trust and test audits. More generated tests do not necessarily mean stronger evidence: a test can merely repeat the implementation or validate its own assumptions. The useful question is whether it checks behaviour that matters.

### [00:19:06] Testing real infrastructure

An infrastructure example makes the discussion concrete. Vincent shows tests that deploy an ephemeral environment, wait for services, inspect Terraform outputs and check logs, traces and metrics. Terratest supplies Go helpers for assertions against real infrastructure; the hosts discuss where shell commands and SDK calls belong.

Kai raises the patience that infrastructure tests require when DNS or services take time to become ready. Vincent distinguishes important behavioural checks from stylistic objections to working generated code. A Datadog fake-intake example shows how a test can verify that telemetry actually arrives.

[slide:3]

At [00:27:46], the discussion returns to Claude Code side agents, mods and cmux. At [00:31:19], they consider moving checks towards deployment gates and smoke tests instead of treating every merge as a global bottleneck.

### [00:32:28] Build versus buy, and the human part of the workflow

Vincent argues that AI makes building internal systems more attractive for large organisations. Kai counters that many teams have limited capacity, uneven adoption and reasons to keep buying established products. They discuss maintenance, company lifecycle and whether an organisation uses AI to increase output or reduce headcount.

From [00:40:02], Kai describes the difficulty of pair programming while juggling several agent sessions. Waiting for one task encourages a switch to another, but a colleague may lose the thread. Skills, plugins and model behaviour keep changing, making it harder to explain or standardise the workflow.

### [00:46:49] New tools meet enterprise release processes

Bun’s releases, Theo’s TypeScript tooling and Tov lead into a discussion about language toolchains, native binaries and worker environments. The hosts are exploring these projects and openly question how they fit together.

Kai brings the conversation back to enterprise needs: secret scanning, security checks and a clear account of what changed between releases. At [00:54:49], they ask whether an agent can act as an independent approver. Vincent raises the possibility that a human can influence its context; both return to human responsibility for understanding and defending a change.

### [01:03:40] Edge runtimes, sandboxes and short-lived agents

Deno joining Cloudflare, celld and JavaScript worker runtimes prompt a discussion of different ways to build and deploy applications. Kai compares the idea with his use of CloudFront Functions; Vincent is interested in environments that can run agent work quickly and with a constrained scope.

[slide:6]

From [01:09:17], they distinguish persistent agents with memory and background tasks from short-lived workers that finish a task and disappear. They consider operating cost, reviewability and the security benefit of reducing how long a compromised process can remain active. The closing conversation revisits model capabilities and costs, then moves through creative websites, Formula One and Kai’s upcoming trip to Malaysia.

## Introduction

This episode (AI Infrastructure, ep. 46 — recorded 14 October 2026) is a wide-ranging conversation between Kai Hendry and Vincent De Smet about how agentic AI is changing developer workflows, engineering roles, testing and observability, build vs buy decisions for enterprises, and emerging runtimes and deployment patterns. The hosts disagree at points about job displacement and the enterprise future; technical details are drawn directly from the guests’ discussion of Anthropic’s engineering blog and many practical examples from their platform work.

[00:00:42] Opening, job impact and Anthropic prompt
- Kai opens with skepticism about AI’s job effects; Vincent pushes back. Kai states, *“I believe AI is going to take away a ton of jobs,”* while Vincent argues many early effects are triangular (displacement, new roles, amplified productivity).
- They surface Anthropic’s recent deep engineering article as a catalyst for the episode: Vincent frames it as a platform/engineering post that challenges Git assumptions and introduces Scion (Anthropic’s monorepo-oriented version control design) and Claude Code (their IDE/harness features).

[00:03:04] Scion, Claude Code, agent architectures and Kiro
- Vincent summarizes Anthropic’s technical takeaways: Scion rethinks the Git client–server symmetry (clients only fetch needed views), assumes always-online clients, and materializes derived views on the server to reduce data transfer at agent scale.
- Claude Code is described as a harness with embedded tools, side-agents and a UI extension model. Vincent contrasts Anthropic’s closed harness with the open Agent Client Protocol (ACP) and Kiro: Kiro advertises UI capabilities to agents (options, artefacts, ask-user flows), which Vincent sees as a cleaner discovery model.
- Kai and Vincent note practical UI/UX differences: Claude Code’s modding, side-agent “you should know” features, and terminal extensions improve agent observability and interaction.

[00:13:55] Engineers’ evolving role, adversarial reviews, tests and Terratest
- Vincent recounts Anthropic’s finding that engineers often acted mainly to veto agent outputs; adversarial reviews produced brittle, over-validated code. The hosts preserve the disagreement: trusting agents more yields productivity but requires skilled engineers to clean overly complex outputs.
- They discuss agent-driven test generation and the need for test audits (OpenClaw skill example). Vincent points to Terratest usage (Go-based assertions for real infrastructure) and nitpicks examples where tests invoke the AWS CLI instead of Terratest SDKs — i.e., agents produce useful artifacts but still need human curation.
- Practical infra testing patterns: local targets, ephemeral environments, smoke tests that block deployment rather than blocking merges, and typed output structures from Terraform state were praised.

[00:32:34] Build vs buy — lifecycle, scale and enterprise constraints
- Vincent argues large AI-native orgs (Anthropic, Uber-scale) are moving toward building platform components (version control, CI/CD) because their scale justifies custom solutions; Kai counters that many enterprises remain buy-oriented because teams are skeletonized and risk-averse.
- They agree adoption varies by company lifecycle and culture: some will outsource while others will internalize capabilities. Vincent warns of a trough of disillusionment as firms move slowly; both note platform teams have a strategic opportunity to embed AI safely for others.

[00:46:54] Tooling, runtimes and the TypeScript-in-Rust thread (Bun, Tov, Deno, Cloudflare, celld)
- The hosts shift to language/runtime news: Bun’s rapid releases (formatter, checker) and Theo’s TypeScript-in-Rust work (Tov/TOV referenced) sparked a conversation about compiling TypeScript in Rust to run faster in isolates and WebAssembly.
- They link this to Deno’s acquisition by Cloudflare and the celld discussion: the set of technologies aims at lightweight, globally-distributed worker sandboxes that make it easier to run agent code at edge/worker scale. Vincent admits he needs to study these deployment models more deeply.

[01:01:24] Agents, identity, compliance and deployment patterns
- The hosts tackle enterprise controls: can agents be approvers? Both are skeptical — human accountability, separation-of-duties and auditability remain required by compliance. Vincent predicts agents will have identities attached to humans rather than be autonomous approvers.
- They discuss ephemeral vs always-on agents: short-lived worker agents (fast, sandboxed edge functions) reduce residency and attack surface, while persistent agents (Kiro/Hermes-style) retain memory and background tasks. Kai flags the pairing and collaboration friction introduced by AI (context switching, new UIs, changing best practices).
- Closing notes: the conversation returns to Anthropic’s lessons (trust but govern agents; move to pre-deploy smoke tests; re-evaluate priors) and to uncertainty about how enterprises will adapt process, release management and compliance as agent workflows mature. They leave with excitement and some caution about the fast pace of change.

- *“we are completely rethinking our priors”*
